blocks.text: 1. Fusion RAG

blocks.alt: A query produces variation 1 and variation 2, which combine through reciprocal rank fusion

blocks.text: Adaptive RAG closed out the core self-correcting patterns of naive, corrective, self, and adaptive RAG. Fusion RAG, which combines results from multiple retrieval passes into one ranked list, shifts focus from choosing one strategy to combining several at once.
It runs several query variations or retrieval methods, then merges their results, a combination technique explored in full throughout this topic.
2. One Query Misses Different Things Than Many
A single query phrasing, as covered generally in Retrieval, retrieves only the chunks that happen to match its exact wording.
Several differently phrased queries surface a wider, complementary set of chunks.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Retrieval approach","Coverage"],"rows":[["Single query","Only chunks matching that exact phrasing"],["Fusion of several queries","Wider, complementary set of chunks"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Generating Multiple Query Variations

blocks.alt: An original query produces variation 1 and variation 2

blocks.text: Building on query expansion as covered generally in Retrieval, the original query is expanded into several related but differently worded versions.
Each variation is retrieved independently before the results are combined.
4. Running Each Variation Through Retrieval

blocks.alt: Variation 1 produces results A while variation 2 produces results B

blocks.text: Each query variation runs through the retriever separately, producing its own ranked chunk list.
Several independent ranked lists now exist for the same underlying question.
5. Reciprocal Rank Fusion Merges The Results

blocks.alt: Results A and results B merge through RRF into merged results

blocks.text: Reciprocal rank fusion combines the separate ranked lists by scoring each chunk on how highly it ranked across all of them.
A chunk appearing near the top of several lists outranks one appearing in just one.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A chunk ranked second in one list and fourth in another accumulates a higher fused score than a chunk ranked first in only one list, because reciprocal rank fusion rewards consistent high ranking across lists.

blocks.text: 6. Why Rank Position Matters More Than Raw Score

blocks.alt: A raw score is compared against rank position

blocks.text: As covered generally with similarity metrics in Embeddings, raw similarity scores are not directly comparable across different retrieval methods.
Rank position within each list is a fair, comparable signal instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal","Comparable across methods"],"rows":[["Raw similarity score","Not directly comparable across different methods"],["Rank position","Comparable regardless of underlying method"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Fusion Combines With Hybrid Search Too
As covered generally with hybrid search in Retrieval, fusion can merge a dense retrieval list and a sparse keyword retrieval list just as easily as multiple query variations.
The same merging logic applies regardless of what produced each ranked list.
8. Multiplying Retrieval Calls Multiplies Cost

blocks.alt: One query is compared against multiple variations at N times the cost

blocks.text: As Advanced RAG covers, each added step costs latency, and running several query variations means several separate retrieval calls.
This is a real multiplier on latency and cost compared with a single retrieval pass.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running four query variations means four separate retrieval calls before fusion even begins, a real multiplier worth weighing against the wider coverage it buys.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Fusion RAG Earns Its Multiplied Retrieval Cost

blocks.alt: A single query missing relevant results points toward fusion RAG

blocks.text: Queries with several valid phrasings or ambiguous wording benefit most from fusion.
Queries with one clear, unambiguous phrasing, by contrast, rarely need multiple variations.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Comparing raw similarity scores across different retrieval methods instead of using rank fusion.
Generating so many query variations that retrieval cost outweighs the coverage benefit.
Forgetting that fusion works on any ranked lists, not only multiple query variations.
Applying fusion to queries with one clear phrasing that did not need multiple variations.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Fusion RAG combines results from multiple retrieval passes into one ranked list.
A single query phrasing misses chunks that differently phrased variations would surface.
The original query is expanded into several variations, each retrieved independently.
Reciprocal rank fusion scores each chunk by how highly it ranked across all lists.
A chunk ranking consistently well across lists outranks one ranking first in only one.
Rank position is a fair, comparable signal since raw scores differ across retrieval methods.
Fusion applies just as well to merging dense and sparse hybrid search results.
Running several query variations multiplies retrieval calls, a real cost against wider coverage.
